title: Understanding Dataset Distillation via Spectral Filtering
one_liner: Dataset distillation works by gradually teaching a tiny synthetic dataset to match the blend of coarse and fine textures that the real data contains.
lead: When you compress a huge dataset into a handful of synthetic images, existing methods freeze their strategy: they either chase blurry shapes or fine details, but never both. This paper shows that all distillation methods work by filtering the frequency information in the data (think: low notes and high notes in a song). The real insight is that the best tiny datasets need BOTH — some low notes, some high. This paper proposes a method that starts learning the coarse textures, then gradually shifts to the fine ones.

paras: Imagine you want to train a neural network (a machine that learns patterns) but you have a million images. Training on all of them is slow and expensive. A beginner's first idea: pick a random subset of, say, 100 images and train on those instead. This almost always fails because the random sample misses rare patterns — it is not representative.

Dataset distillation solves this differently: instead of picking real images, you CREATE a tiny set of fake images that the model learns from just as well as the full dataset. But there is a puzzle: different methods for creating these fake images use different recipes. Some methods make the fake images blurry and capture only large-scale shapes. Others make sharp, fine-grained textures. The existing methods are also locked in: once you pick your recipe, you are stuck with it throughout training. You cannot adapt.

callout.html: The paper reveals that each distillation method is secretly filtering the frequencies of data (low frequencies for blur, high frequencies for detail), and proposes a method that gradually shifts from low to high frequencies during training.

steps.text: Compute what textures are actually present (the frequency spectrum of real images).
Set the filter to capture only blurry, large-scale patterns (low frequencies).
Train a set of 50–100 fake images to match what that filter sees.
Slowly adjust the filter to emphasize fine-grained textures (high frequencies) over time.
The synthetic images end up encoding both structure and detail, no single aspect is starved.

paras: The paper changes the filter function itself, making it dynamic rather than fixed. In all prior distillation methods, you pick one 'filter recipe' at the start (e.g., 'capture low frequencies') and that is what you optimize for the entire time. This paper's method adjusts the filter as training progresses, gradually turning the dial from 'blurry' to 'sharp'.
object.object: the filter control knob (the dial that chooses how much blur versus detail)

hidden.name: How much low-frequency versus high-frequency information the synthetic images contain
paras: Each image can be decomposed into frequencies: low frequencies are slow changes (a red wall, a blue sky), high frequencies are rapid changes (a crack, a leaf vein, a face wrinkle). The paper measures this using the eigenvalues of two matrices: the feature-feature correlation (the pattern of which features tend to appear together) and the feature-label correlation (which features predict the label). The filter function is essentially a control knob: turn it one way and the synthetic data matches only the low-frequency patterns; turn it the other way and it matches the high-frequency patterns.

The paper estimates this hidden quantity by looking at the actual eigenvalues of these correlation matrices at each layer of the network, and applying the filter function to them. By gradually adjusting the control knob throughout training, the method ensures the synthetic data captures the full spectrum.

heat.caption: Darker cell means more emphasis. Early training (left) emphasizes low frequencies; late training (right) emphasizes high frequencies.

reads.html: Imagine a blurry photo and a sharp one of the same scene. The blurry photo tells you the large shapes; the sharp one tells you the texture. Dataset distillation needs both kinds of information mixed in the tiny synthetic dataset.

The feature-feature correlation matrix (FFC) and feature-label correlation matrix (FLC) encode which patterns coexist and which patterns predict the target. Applying a filter function to their eigenvalues is equivalent to amplifying certain frequency bands and suppressing others.

mechanism.h2: Why gradually shifting filters works better
paras: Here is the core reason: when you train a neural network on a dataset, it learns in stages. Early in training, the network is naive — it benefits most from learning the big, obvious patterns (low frequencies: is this a cat or dog? rough size and color). Once it understands those, it needs finer details (high frequencies: eye shape, fur texture). If you force a synthetic dataset to encode only the fine details from the start, the network has nothing to learn first; it is overwhelmed. If you encode only the coarse patterns, the network finishes early but never learns to distinguish similar things.

The paper's method mimics how a good teacher works: start by explaining the big picture, then gradually zoom in on the details. The filter parameter is adjusted during training (set lower values of beta early, higher values late). This lets the synthetic data serve the network's actual learning process. The result is that a smaller synthetic dataset can now replace a much larger real dataset, because every synthetic image is teaching something the network needs to learn at that moment.

stages.s: Train synthetic images to match low frequencies

math.words: For each batch, the loss is the squared difference between the filtered real correlation matrix and the filtered synthetic correlation matrix, plus a term that matches the features themselves, plus a classification loss.
math.equation: Loss = sum over batches [ (FFC_real + beta*I)^-1 - (FFC_synth + beta*I)^-1 ]^2 + (FFC_real + beta*I)^-1 * FLC_real - (FFC_synth + beta*I)^-1 * FLC_synth + cross_entropy_loss(synthetic_output, labels)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Loss_filter = squared difference of these matrices ≈ (0.167-0.206)^2 + (0.033-0.023)^2 ≈ 0.0024
Later, Batch 3 (beta=0.01): the filter barely dampens; high frequencies dominate.
The weight on high-frequency components grows as training progresses.

math.note: Beta starts high (emphasizing global structure), then shrinks (letting high frequencies through), mirroring the network's learning trajectory from big picture to fine detail.

bars.h2: Comparison: fixed filter vs. curriculum filter

charts.title: Fixed low-pass filter (old methods)
charts.note: Captures blur well but misses texture; needs more synthetic images to recover detail.

charts.title: Curriculum Frequency Matching (this paper)
charts.note: Reaches similar accuracy with fewer images because it teaches the network in the right order.

items.html: If the filter shifts too quickly, the synthetic data jumps from coarse to fine without properly covering intermediate frequencies. The network gets confused.
If you reduce the low-frequency weight too fast, the synthetic images forget the coarse patterns they learned and try to over-optimize for high frequencies. The network loses its foundation.
If the initial synthetic images do not learn the low-frequency patterns well enough, shifting to high frequencies later amplifies noise instead of detail.
When the filter control is reduced gradually (starting at high values, then 0.5, then 0.01 over batches), the synthetic images learn in stages and converge to both structure and texture.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple convolutional network (e.g., ResNet-9 on CIFAR-10). Start with a real training set (50,000 images) and measure accuracy on a test set (10,000 images). Then create 100 synthetic images optimized using the curriculum frequency matching method. Plot the test accuracy of models trained on these 100 synthetic images. Compare against baseline methods (low-pass-only, high-pass-only). The demo should show that the curriculum method reaches accuracy comparable to baseline within fewer epochs, because it is teaching the network in the order the network naturally learns.
demo.closing: The metric that matters: how many synthetic images does each method need to close the accuracy gap to 90% of the full-data accuracy? Curriculum matching should win with the fewest images, showing that it is compressing the dataset more efficiently by teaching in the right order.
